title: Mock 6 · Tough Numericals I
blurb: Exam-pressure set: continuous-compounding fair value, arbitrage profit, parity mispricing, delta rebalancing, open positions and MWPL.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about OTC derivatives is NOT correct?
options: Contracts are tailor-made to fit the needs of the counterparties
Counterparty credit risk is managed centrally by a clearing corporation
Transactions are private, with little or no disclosure to the market
There are no formal centralised limits on positions, leverage or margining
questions.explanation: In OTC markets, counterparty (credit) risk management is decentralised and located within individual institutions. A clearing corporation guarantee is a feature of exchange-traded contracts.
hints: True of OTC contracts.
Correct choice (the false statement): OTC risk management is decentralised.
True of OTC contracts.
True of OTC contracts.

questions.q: Arrange the launch of the following equity derivatives in India in chronological order: (P) stock futures, (Q) index options, (R) index futures, (S) stock options.
questions.explanation: Index futures came in June 2000, index options in June 2001, stock options in July 2001 and stock futures in November 2001, giving R → Q → S → P.
hints: Stock futures came last, not second.
Index futures came first.
Correct: R (Jun 2000), Q (Jun 2001), S (Jul 2001), P (Nov 2001).
Index options (June) came before stock options (July).

questions.q: An order book shows best buy orders at ₹9.80 and sell orders of 1,000 @ ₹9.90, 1,500 @ ₹10.00 and 1,000 @ ₹10.10. What is the impact cost of a market buy order for 2,000 shares?
hints: This measures from the best ask (9.90), not the ideal price.
This is the workbook's figure for a 1,500-share order, not 2,000.
Double-counted.

questions.q: Under SEBI's four-tranche approach for a non-benchmark index, the top constituent's weight is 28% and the target is 20%. What will its adjusted weight be after the first monthly tranche?
questions.explanation: The excess of 8% is spread over 4 tranches, giving (28 − 20)/4 = 2% in month 1, so the weight becomes 26%. Weights are re-evaluated before each later tranche.
hints: That would be a single-tranche adjustment.
That reduces by 4% (two tranches' worth).
Correct: 28 − 2 = 26%.
That reduces by only 1%.

questions.q: An index is at 24,000. The risk-free rate is 7% p.a. and the dividend yield is 1% p.a. Using continuous compounding, F = S·e^((r−q)T), the fair value of a 60-day futures contract is:
hints: This ignores the dividend yield.
This uses discrete compounding (1.06^(60/365)).
This is a rounded simple approximation.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹2,000 and its 3-month futures at ₹2,070. The cost of carry is 10% p.a. (continuous) and the lot size is 250. Ignoring transaction costs, what is the arbitrage profit per lot from cash-and-carry?
hints: This ignores the financing cost (uses 70 × 250).
This is the carrying cost, not the profit.
This uses a rounded fair value of 2,050.

questions.q: A fund manager holds a portfolio worth ₹2 crore with a beta of 0.8. Nifty futures trade at 24,000 with a lot size of 75. To hedge market risk fully, the manager should:
hints: This ignores beta (2 cr / 18 lakh = 11.1).
Buying futures increases exposure.
Correct: 8.89, rounded to 9, short.
This under-hedges.

questions.q: An investor plans to buy 1,000 shares in a month and goes long one lot (1,000) of stock futures at ₹640. On the purchase date the stock is at ₹700 and the futures at ₹702. He buys the shares and squares off the futures. What is his effective cost per share?
questions.explanation: Futures gain = (702 − 640) × 1,000 = ₹62,000. Net cost = 7,00,000 − 62,000 = 6,38,000, i.e. ₹638 per share, close to the locked futures price.
hints: This ignores the futures gain.
Close, but the basis change makes it ₹638, not exactly 640.
This adds the gain instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Day 1: P buys 200 contracts from Q (both open). Day 2: R buys 150 from S (both open). Day 3: P sells 200 contracts to Q (both close). What are the open interest at the end of Day 3 and the trading volume on Day 3?
questions.explanation: OI: 200 → 350 → when P and Q both close 200, it falls to 150. Day 3 volume = 200 contracts traded that day.
hints: Correct: OI 150, day volume 200.
OI falls when both sides close.
Volume is per day, not cumulative.
OI counts outstanding contracts on one side only.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the cost of carry model is NOT correct?
options: It assumes the underlying can be sold short
It assumes no taxes and no transaction costs
It cannot be applied to assets that are not storable
It is better suited to futures than forwards because it accounts for margins
questions.explanation: The model ignores margins, which is why the workbook says it is suitable for pricing forwards rather than futures.
hints: A stated assumption.
A stated assumption.
True: a non-storable asset cannot be carried.
Correct choice (false): margins are ignored, so it suits forwards better.

questions.q: Consider: (I) The delta of a long put lies between 0 and −1. (II) Vega is negative for a long call. (III) Gamma measures the change in delta for a unit change in the underlying. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I is true (long put delta is 0 to −1). II is false (vega is positive for long calls and long puts). III is true (gamma = change in delta / unit change in price).
hints: II is false.
Correct: I and III.
II is false.
II is false.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹1,060. A trader buys a 1,000-strike put at ₹6. At expiry the stock settles at ₹960. What is his return on investment (net profit ÷ premium)?
questions.explanation: Payoff = 1,000 − 960 = 40; net profit = 40 − 6 = 34; ROI = 34/6 = 567%. Deep OTM puts give the highest ROI on a sharp fall.
hints: That is the ROI of a different (1,050-strike) put.
This uses the gross payoff (40/6).
34 is the profit in rupees, not the ROI.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹2,480. The 2,400-strike call is at ₹112 and the lot size is 300. What is the total time value contained in one lot of this call?
hints: That is the intrinsic value per lot.
That is the total premium per lot.
That is per share, not per lot.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is NOT true?
options: Options are called wasting assets because their time value decays to zero by expiry
An increase in the strike price lowers a call's value and raises a put's value
Option sellers need not pay margin because they receive the premium upfront
ATM options carry the highest uncertainty among ITM, ATM and OTM options
questions.explanation: Option sellers have an obligation and potentially unlimited loss, so they must pay margin. It is buyers who pay no margin.
hints: True.
True.
Correct choice (false): writers must pay margin.
True: a small move can tip an ATM option either way.

questions.q: You write a 760-strike call at ₹18 (lot size 1,200). At expiry the stock settles at ₹790. What are your net P&L and the break-even price?
questions.explanation: Short call P&L = 18 − (790 − 760) = −12 per share × 1,200 = −₹14,400. BEP = X + P = 760 + 18 = 778, the same as for a long call.
hints: Correct: −₹14,400 and BEP 778.
This ignores the premium and subtracts it in the BEP.
This counts only the premium received.
The call BEP adds the premium (X + P).

questions.q: A put option has a delta of −0.35. If the underlying falls by ₹8, the put premium will approximately:
questions.explanation: Change in premium = delta × ΔS = (−0.35) × (−8) = +2.80. Puts gain when the underlying falls.
hints: The sign is wrong: puts gain on a fall.
Correct: rises by ₹2.80.
That assumes a delta of −1.
That is the change for a ₹1 move, with the wrong sign.

questions.q: A trader sells a 1,500-strike call at ₹48 and buys a 1,560-strike call at ₹20 (same expiry). Which describes the position correctly?
questions.explanation: Bear call spread: net credit = 48 − 20 = 28 (max profit). Max loss = (1,560 − 1,500) − 28 = 32. BEP = lower strike + credit = 1,528.
hints: Correct: 28, 32 and 1,528.
Profit and loss are swapped.
Max loss must deduct the credit received.
This treats it as a bull spread.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹2,010. A 1-month European 2,000 call trades at ₹70, the interest rate is 7% p.a. (continuous), and the 2,000 put trades at ₹42. Using put-call parity, what arbitrage exists and what is the approximate risk-free profit per share?
options: Sell the put and the stock, buy the call; about ₹6.37
No arbitrage; the put is fairly priced
Buy the put and the stock, sell the call; about ₹6.37
Buy the put and the stock, sell the call; about ₹28
questions.explanation: Fair p = c + X·e^(−rt) − S = 70 + 2,000 × e^(−0.07/12) − 2,010 ≈ 48.37. The market put (42) is cheap, so buy the put and the stock, sell the call, and borrow the outlay. Profit ≈ 48.37 − 42 = ₹6.37.
hints: You sell the overpriced leg, but the put here is underpriced.
The fair put is about 48.37 against 42 in the market, so a gap exists.
Correct: buy the underpriced put (+ stock, short call); gain about ₹6.37.
The right legs, but the gain is the mispricing (≈6.37), not the call-put difference.

questions.q: A trader sells a 1,100-strike call at ₹14 and a 1,000-strike put at ₹11. What is the net P&L per share if the stock settles at ₹1,140 on expiry?
questions.explanation: Short strangle: premium collected = 25. Call loss = 1,140 − 1,100 = 40; the put expires worthless. Net = 25 − 40 = −₹15 (upper BEP 1,125 has been crossed).
hints: That is the maximum profit (if the price stays between 1,000 and 1,100).
This ignores the premiums collected.
This counts only the put premium.

questions.q: A trader is short 15 lots of calls (delta 0.40) and long 6 lots of futures, which is delta-neutral (equal lot sizes). The underlying rallies and the call delta rises to 0.60. To restore delta neutrality, he must:
questions.explanation: New option delta = −0.60 × 15 = −9 lots. He holds +6, so he needs +3 more lots of long futures (9 in total).
hints: Selling increases the negative delta.
Delta has changed, so the hedge must be adjusted.
9 is the total needed, not the additional amount.
Correct: buy 3 more (6 → 9).

questions.q: A client is long 200 futures, long 600 calls (delta 0.4) and long 300 puts (delta −0.6) on the same stock. What is the client's Future-Equivalent (delta-adjusted) open interest?
questions.explanation: FutEq OI = 200 × 1 + 600 × 0.4 + 300 × (−0.6) = 200 + 240 − 180 = 260. The old notional measure would have been 1,100.
hints: That is the old notional OI (simple sum).
This adds the put delta instead of subtracting it.
This omits the futures position.

questions.q: A company announces a rights issue of 1 share for every 5 held at ₹180. The closing price on the last cum-date is ₹240. What are the benefit per share (E) and the adjustment factor?
hints: Correct: E = 10, AF = 0.9583.
This uses the benefit per right entitlement (60) as E.
This divides by 5 instead of 6.
The AF is inverted.

questions.q: A stock closed at ₹400 the day before its board announced a dividend of ₹10 per share. What happens to an existing 420-strike call option?
options: No change: the dividend is ordinary
Strike adjusted to ₹410 from the ex-dividend date
questions.explanation: 10/400 = 2.5%, which is above 2%, so the dividend is extraordinary. The full dividend is deducted from all strikes: 420 − 10 = ₹410, effective from the ex-dividend date.
hints: The 2% threshold is crossed (2.5%), so it is extraordinary.
The full dividend amount is reduced, not a percentage of the strike.
Strikes are reduced, not increased.

questions.q: For a futures trade with a value of ₹18,00,000, what are the STT (on the sell side) and the stamp duty (on the buy side), per the workbook rates?
questions.explanation: STT on futures = 0.05% × 18,00,000 = ₹900 (seller). Stamp duty on futures = 0.002% × 18,00,000 = ₹36 (buyer).
hints: These use the options rates (0.15% and 0.003%).
The stamp duty uses the options rate (0.003%).
The STT is wrong.
Correct: ₹900 STT and ₹36 stamp duty.

questions.q: A clearing member clears for TM1 and TM2 in one contract. TM1: pro buy 800/sell 300; client X buy 200/sell 500; client Y buy 400/sell 100. TM2: pro buy 100/sell 600; client Z buy 700/sell 200. What is the CM's open position?
questions.explanation: TM1: pro +500, X −300, Y +300, giving long 800 and short 300. TM2: pro −500, Z +500, giving long 500 and short 500. CM: long 800 + 500 = 1,300; short 300 + 500 = 800.
hints: Correct: long 1,300, short 800.
Client positions are not netted against each other.
Gross buys and sells are not used; net each account first.
That is TM1 alone.

questions.q: A company has 50 crore shares held by non-promoters. What is its MWPL, and above what aggregate open interest will no fresh positions be allowed from the next trading day?
questions.explanation: MWPL = 20% of free-float shares = 10 crore. The ban applies when aggregate OI exceeds 95% of MWPL = 9.5 crore shares. Normal trading resumes at or below 80% (8 crore).
hints: This uses 10% instead of 20%.
8 crore is the 80% resumption level, not the ban trigger.
Correct: 10 crore MWPL; ban above 9.5 crore.
This uses 30%.

questions.q: Mr. A holds an ITM long put (strike ₹250) and, on expiry day, buys the same shares in the cash market at ₹238 through the same TM-CM. The settlement price is ₹240. Under net settlement, what does he receive per share?
questions.explanation: Under net settlement of cash and F&O on expiry, there is no separate pay-in and delivery. He receives the strike price minus his purchase price: 250 − 238 = ₹12.
hints: This uses the settlement price instead of his purchase price.
This is just the gap between settlement price and purchase price.
He does not receive the full strike, because the share purchase is netted.

questions.q: While computing a clearing member's net worth for derivatives membership, which of the following is NOT deducted as a non-allowable asset?
questions.explanation: Net worth = capital + free reserves minus non-allowable assets (fixed assets, pledged securities, member's card, unlisted securities, bad deliveries, doubtful debts, prepaid expenses, intangibles, 30% of marketable securities).
hints: Deducted.
Deducted.
Deducted.
Correct choice: free reserves are ADDED, not deducted.

questions.q: A buyer paid ₹80 per unit as premium for 500 units of a stock option. On the balance sheet date, the prevailing premium is ₹55. What provision for loss should the buyer make?
questions.explanation: The buyer provides for the excess of premium paid over the prevailing premium: (80 − 55) × 500 = ₹12,500, since he could square off at ₹55.
hints: That is the current market value of the option.
A loss must be provided for (prudence).
That is the full premium paid.

questions.q: A broker's staff report a client's transactions as suspicious to the Principal Officer. Which course of action is consistent with the workbook?
options: Inform the client immediately and close the account
Continue dealing with the client as normal and do not disclose the report to the client
Freeze all the client's securities until FIU-IND responds
Ask the client to explain the transactions in writing before reporting
questions.explanation: Dealings should continue as normal until told otherwise, and the client must not be told of the report or suspicion. Suspension happens only in exceptional circumstances.
hints: Tipping off the client is prohibited.
Correct: continue normally and do not tip off.
Suspension is only for exceptional cases.
Questioning the client risks tipping them off.
